name: Mind · Cognitive Biases
description: Spot the bias behind everyday moments: sunk costs, anchoring, the Dunning–Kruger effect and 27 more quirks of the mind.

cards.front: You only notice news that agrees with you.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Peter Wason's 1960 experiment: guess the rule behind a triple of numbers

cards.front: You sit through a bad movie because you already paid for the ticket.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Also called the Concorde fallacy: Britain and France kept funding a doomed jet

cards.front: The first price you see sets how every later price feels.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Tversky and Kahneman, 1974: a wheel rigged to stop on 10 or 65 swayed UN guesses

cards.front: A beginner is sure they're already as good as the experts.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: David Dunning and Justin Kruger, 1999: weaker performers rated themselves too high

cards.front: After a shark-attack headline, you fear swimming more than driving.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Tversky and Kahneman, early 1970s: what comes to mind fast feels more likely

cards.front: You join the long queue just because it is long.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: “Jump on the bandwagon” dates from Zachary Taylor's 1848 campaign

cards.front: You learn a new word, then it seems to be everywhere.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Named in a 1994 letter by Terry Mullen; Arnold Zwicky coined “frequency illusion” in 2005

cards.front: Red came up five times in a row, so black must be due.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Monte Carlo, 1913: roulette landed on black 26 times in a row

cards.front: You think everyone noticed the stain on your shirt.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Coined by Gilovich, Medvec and Savitsky; an embarrassing T-shirt makes it stronger

cards.front: You love the shelf you built yourself, wobble and all.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Norton, Mochon and Ariely, 2011: buyers paid 63% more for self-assembled furniture

cards.front: You assume the good-looking candidate is also the smartest.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Edward Thorndike coined the term and gave the evidence in 1920

cards.front: One harsh comment outweighs ten compliments.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Baumeister and colleagues reviewed it: bad events grab more attention than good ones

cards.front: After the match you say, “I knew they'd lose all along.”
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Baruch Fischhoff studied it in the 1970s as “creeping determinism”

cards.front: “Ten minutes,” you say, and an hour later you are still going.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Kahneman and Tversky, 1979; the Sydney Opera House opened a decade late

cards.front: You copy successful founders and never study the failed ones.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Abraham Wald studied returning WWII planes to decide where to add armor

cards.front: Their lateness is laziness; your own lateness is traffic.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Lee Ross coined it in 1977, a decade after Jones and Harris's Castro-essay study

cards.front: Divorce, illness, accidents: those happen to other people, not you.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Also called unrealistic optimism; found across cultures, ages and genders

cards.front: Losing $20 stings more than finding $20 feels good.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Kahneman and Tversky coined it in 1979; losses weigh about twice as much as gains

cards.front: “90% survive” sounds better to you than “10% die”.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Tversky and Kahneman's 1981 paper, with the Asian disease problem, tested it

cards.front: A pointless middle option makes the pricey one look like a bargain.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: In Ariely's Economist test, nobody chose the $125 print-only decoy

cards.front: You won't sell your old mug for what you would pay to buy it.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Richard Thaler coined it in 1980; in mug experiments owners would not swap

cards.front: You keep the default plan because changing feels like effort.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Samuelson and Zeckhauser showed it in 1988 with decision questionnaires

cards.front: You like a song more after hearing it a few times.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Robert Zajonc's 1960s experiments showed that familiarity breeds liking

cards.front: A vague horoscope feels like it was written just for you.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Forer gave 39 students the same “personal” profile; Meehl named it for P. T. Barnum

cards.front: A task you left unfinished keeps nagging at you.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Kurt Lewin noticed a waiter recalled only unpaid orders; Bluma Zeigarnik studied it

cards.front: You rate a holiday by its best moment and how it ended.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Kahneman and Redelmeier, 1996: colonoscopy patients' memories followed peak and end

cards.front: You explain it badly because you forgot what not knowing felt like.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Coined in 1989 by economists Camerer, Loewenstein and Weber

cards.front: You assume most people share your opinion, because your friends do.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Defined by Ross, Greene and House in 1977

cards.front: Told “don't touch”, you suddenly want to touch it.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: Jack Brehm developed the theory: threats to your freedom of choice provoke pushback

cards.front: Once you've bought it, you remember it as the better choice.
cards.label: bias
cards.hook: In Henkel and Mather's used-car study, people favoured the car they had “chosen”
